Dialectic of Enlightenment is one of those books that make you think even if you disagree with much in the content (and defending the authenticity of art against kitsch isn't what got us into our current predicament). He features strongly also in Alex Ross's The Rest is Noise: Listening to the Twentieth Century and Scruton's (who was also a composer among many other things) The Aesthetics of Music and Understanding Music: Philosophy and Interpretation.

Regarding doubt and the Twitter topic of whether someone on the right should read leftist authors, it is my personal experience while travelling across the political spectrum from the left to the 'far-right' (the mind aspiring to rationality dragging the liberal heart along) that the variety and standard in literature declines. And I'm now talking about the literature of the past 200 or so years (I don't have a high opinion of the leftist authors of today, and I have read many of them). It is barren on the far-right historically and today. And the quality and depth of the thinking itself often leaves you unaffected. You may agree with the conclusions and the 'worldview' but the thinking and the literary merits in themselves are another thing. It is the contrary to someone like Adorno, or Charles Taylor (a liberal catholic Canadian philosopher, see Sources of the Self) or Kafka or Zweig (another early 20th century Jewish author) or Tolstoy who you can read for the thinking and/or literary quality alone irrespective of how much you do or don't agree with them. So while I am politically far-right (population realist, for remigration etc.) the clear majority of my favourite writers and thinkers remain far behind to the left. So I would lie if I tried to deny the major doubts I have about the 'far-right' outside of the core political positions, as a 'high-cultural' and literary force.

Persistent elasticity and tensile strength

White/cream colour rather than red/yellow
Luminal conformity and branching
Absence of gelatinous texture

Comparison with classical antemortem thrombi
The anomalous intravascular casts (AICs) documented in this study differ in several fundamental respects from recognised antemortem thrombi. Classical arterial or venous thrombi typically demonstrate prominent Lines of Zahn, extensive cellular entrapment, and a laminated structure reflecting repeated cycles of fibrin deposition and cellular incorporation under pulsatile flow (Bancroft, 2019). In contrast, the AIC specimens showed only partial or regionally restricted Lines of Zahn, and cellular inclusions were sparse, with many areas nearly acellular. Additionally, the AICs exhibited an unusual mechanical elasticity and tensile coherence not characteristic of fibrin-dominant thrombi.
Although the presence of partial lamination implies some formation under active circulation, the structural uniformity of the fibrin bundles, the minimal entrapment of erythrocytes and leukocytes, and the predominance of dense, homogeneous fibre networks collectively distinguish these casts from the classical thrombus phenotype.
Comparison with canonical postmortem clots
The differences between AICs and postmortem coagula were even more pronounced. Postmortem clots—whether “currant-jelly” or “chicken fat”—are gelatinous, friable, non-adherent, and lack flow-derived structures such as Lines of Zahn. They readily conform to the shape of the cavity in which they settle and commonly wash out during dissection. Because postmortem coagula lack cross-linked fibrin architecture and undergo passive sedimentation rather than active polymerisation, they cannot develop the elastic, tension-bearing properties observed in AICs. Importantly, no known postmortem interval changes or decomposition processes generate elastic, laminated, lumen-conforming structures, indicating that the features observed here cannot plausibly arise as postmortem artefacts.
